summary.text: For \(n=162178349052694\), the number \(a(n)+4=1813934020268071832273\) lies strictly between \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\). It is a Sierpiński number because it is odd and greater than one, while the residue classes \(r\equiv0\pmod2,3\pmod4,1\pmod8,5\pmod{16},29\pmod{32},45\pmod{48},29\pmod{48},13\pmod{96}\) cover every exponent and make \(1813934020268071832273\cdot2^r+1\) divisible respectively by \(3,5,17,257,65537,97,673,193\), hence composite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9454129+11184810n.
\]
Recall that an odd integer \(k>1\) is a Sierpiński number if, for every positive integer \(r\), the number
\[
k2^r+1
\]
is composite. We will exhibit a particular index \(N\) for which there is another Sierpiński number strictly between \(a(N)\) and \(a(N)+28\).

Set
\[
N=162178349052694
\]
and
\[
K=1813934020268071832273.
\]
Direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
&=9454129+11184810\cdot162178349052694\\
&=1813934020268071832269.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
K=a(N)+4.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(N)<K<a(N)+28,
\]
since the differences from the lower and upper endpoints are respectively \(4\) and \(24\). It remains to prove that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

We use the following elementary periodic-divisibility observation. Suppose that integers \(p,m,e\) satisfy \(p>1\), \(m>0\),
\[
2^m\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and
\[
K2^e+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
If \(r\equiv e\pmod m\), write \(r=qm+e\). Then
\[
2^r=2^{qm+e}=(2^m)^q2^e\equiv2^e\pmod p,
\]
and consequently
\[
K2^r+1\equiv K2^e+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Thus \(p\mid K2^r+1\). If in addition \(p<K\), this divisor is proper and nontrivial: indeed \(p>1\), while
\[
p<K<K2^r+1
\]
for every \(r\geq0\). Therefore \(K2^r+1\) cannot be prime.

For the present \(K\), we use the following eight triples \((p,m,e)\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p&m&e\\ \hline
3&2&0\\
5&4&3\\
17&8&1\\
257&16&5\\
65537&32&29\\
97&48&45\\
673&48&29\\
193&96&13
\end{array}
\]
We now check both required congruences for every row.

First, the periodicity congruences \(2^m\equiv1\pmod p\) in the first five rows follow from
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^2-1&=3,\\
2^4-1&=15=3\cdot5,\\
2^8-1&=255=15\cdot17,\\
2^{16}-1&=65535=255\cdot257,\\
2^{32}-1&=4294967295=65535\cdot65537.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the remaining rows, short repeated-squaring computations give the needed congruences. Modulo \(97\),
\[
2^8\equiv62,\qquad 2^{16}\equiv61,\qquad 2^{32}\equiv35,
\]
so
\[
2^{48}=2^{32}2^{16}\equiv35\cdot61=2135=22\cdot97+1\equiv1\pmod{97}.
\]
Modulo \(673\),
\[
2^8\equiv256,\qquad 2^{16}\equiv255,\qquad 2^{32}\equiv417,
\]
and hence
\[
2^{48}\equiv417\cdot255=106335=158\cdot673+1\equiv1\pmod{673}.
\]
Finally, modulo \(193\), repeated squaring gives
\[
2^8\equiv63,\qquad 2^{16}\equiv109,\qquad
2^{32}\equiv108,\qquad 2^{64}\equiv84.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^{96}=2^{64}2^{32}\equiv84\cdot108=9072=47\cdot193+1\equiv1\pmod{193}.
\]
This establishes \(2^m\equiv1\pmod p\) for all eight rows.

Next we check \(K2^e+1\equiv0\pmod p\). The reductions of \(K\) modulo the eight divisors are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p&K\bmod p&2^e\bmod p\\ \hline
3&2&1\\
5&3&3\\
17&8&2\\
257&8&32\\
65537&65529=-8&57345\\
97&89=-8&85\\
673&652=-21&641=-32\\
193&92&86
\end{array}
\]
For completeness, the reductions of \(K\) can be read from the exact divisions
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=3\cdot604644673422690610757+2,\\
K&=5\cdot362786804053614366454+3,\\
K&=17\cdot106702001192239519545+8,\\
K&=257\cdot7058109028280435145+8,\\
K&=65537\cdot27678014255581912+65529,\\
K&=97\cdot18700350724413111672+89,\\
K&=673\cdot2695295721052112677+652,\\
K&=193\cdot9398621866673947317+92.
\end{aligned}
\]
The powers in the third column are obtained by ordinary repeated squaring. Substituting the displayed residues makes the divisibility especially transparent:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p& (K\bmod p)(2^e\bmod p)+1\\ \hline
3&2\cdot1+1=3\\
5&3\cdot3+1=10=2\cdot5\\
17&8\cdot2+1=17\\
257&8\cdot32+1=257\\
65537&(-8)\cdot57345+1=-458759=-7\cdot65537\\
97&(-8)\cdot85+1=-679=-7\cdot97\\
673&(-21)(-32)+1=673\\
193&92\cdot86+1=7913=41\cdot193.
\end{array}
\]
Therefore \(p\mid K2^e+1\) in every row.

We now show that the associated residue classes cover every exponent \(r\). The classes are
\[
\begin{split}
r&\equiv0\pmod2,\\
r&\equiv3\pmod4,\\
r&\equiv1\pmod8,\\
r&\equiv5\pmod{16},\\
r&\equiv29\pmod{32},\\
r&\equiv45\pmod{48},\\
r&\equiv29\pmod{48},\\
r&\equiv13\pmod{96}.
\end{split}
\]
Their exhaustiveness follows by a successive parity split. If \(r\) is even, it is in the first class. Suppose that \(r\) is odd. Modulo \(4\), it is either \(1\) or \(3\); in the latter case it is in the second class. If it is \(1\pmod4\), then modulo \(8\) it is either \(1\) or \(5\); the first possibility is the third class. If it is \(5\pmod8\), then modulo \(16\) it is either \(5\) or \(13\); the first possibility is the fourth class. If it is \(13\pmod{16}\), then modulo \(32\) it is either \(13\) or \(29\); the latter is the fifth class.

Only the case \(r\equiv13\pmod{32}\) remains. Since \(96=3\cdot32\), the three possible residues modulo \(96\) are
\[
13,\quad45,\quad77.
\]
If \(r\equiv13\pmod{96}\), it is in the eighth class. If \(r\equiv45\pmod{96}\), then \(r\equiv45\pmod{48}\), so it is in the sixth class. If \(r\equiv77\pmod{96}\), then \(r\equiv29\pmod{48}\), so it is in the seventh class. Thus every nonnegative integer exponent belongs to at least one of the eight classes.

Take any positive integer \(r\). Select a row of the table whose residue class contains \(r\). By the periodic-divisibility observation, the corresponding \(p\) divides \(K2^r+1\). Every divisor in the table is at least \(3\) and at most \(65537\), whereas
\[
K=1813934020268071832273.
\]
Thus
\[
1<p<K<K2^r+1.
\]
So \(p\) is a nontrivial proper divisor of \(K2^r+1\), proving that \(K2^r+1\) is composite. This holds for every positive \(r\).

Finally, \(K\) is greater than \(1\), and it is odd because its final digit is \(3\). Hence \(K\) satisfies every condition in the definition of a Sierpiński number.

We have therefore found, at the explicit index \(N=162178349052694\), the Sierpiński number
\[
K=1813934020268071832273=a(N)+4
\]
strictly between \(a(N)\) and \(a(N)+28\). Consequently those two endpoint numbers are not consecutive Sierpiński numbers. This single index contradicts the assertion that they are consecutive for every \(n\geq0\), and therefore disproves the conjecture.
